articleSummary: Meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) can affect all ages. In adults who have not been vaccinated, risk depends on exposure, immune status, and local epidemiology. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets and saliva, with high risk in close, prolonged contact—living in dormitories or barracks, sharing meals, or direct contact with an infected person’s secretions. Carriage without illness is possible but does not guarantee disease. International age distributions differ; do not extrapolate foreign data to Vietnam. For those with close exposure, contact healthcare promptly; vaccination history should be reviewed.

articleSummary: Systematic review across Africa finds 79.3% of circulating currency notes contaminated with bacteria (95% CI 60.9–90.4%), based on 12 studies and 2,003 notes; 1,455 notes were contaminated (crude 72.6%). articleHeadline: Retrospective study links infections and outcome risks in Good syndrome
articleSummary: Good syndrome (thymoma with hypogammaglobulinemia and opportunistic infections) evaluated at Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China, from January 2015 to December 2024. Autoimmune diseases were present in 44.4%, and another malignancy in 7.4%; radiotherapy or chemotherapy for thymoma occurred in 25.9%. The cohort’s mean age at onset was 57.8 years (SD 9.3), with 37% male; all patients experienced infection during follow-up. Cox regression linked older age (HR 1.270 per year, 95% CI 1.042–1.548, p=0.018) and each additional day of pre-infection corticosteroid use (HR 1.049, 95% CI 1.004–1.095, p=0.033) to worse outcomes. articleHeadline: Class closures associated with fewer norovirus cases in Xi'an schools
articleSummary: Norovirus outbreaks in Xi’an educational settings (schools and kindergartens) reported to the Xi’an Center for Disease Control and Prevention from Oct 2020–Feb 2023: 61 outbreaks analyzed, with 44 meeting complete-data criteria (72.13%). Limitations: observational, not randomized; findings specific to Xi’an educational settings.

articleSummary: Newcastle disease outbreak confirmed at a commercial turkey farm in Nova Itaberaba, western Santa Catarina, Brazil. The facility houses about 6,000 birds to be sacrificed after routine surveillance detected infection; a 10-km restriction zone includes Nova Itaberaba, Nova Erechim, Águas Frias, and Coronel Freitas. In total, 133 nearby farms are under surveillance and around 1,600 other rural properties will be visited; 40 Olho Bom vehicles patrol within the radius. The Emergency status was declared by state authorities and the Federal Veterinary Service halted poultry movement. Lab confirmation came from LFDA-SP on Sunday 18, announced Monday 19. The virus appeared during routine checks; no birds have left the site since housing. The disease, caused by avian paramyxovirus type 1 (APMV-1), spreads via aerosols and contaminated materials; human infection is rare, usually mild conjunctivitis. Trade responses include Mexico banning all Brazilian avian products, and China and Chile restricting Santa Catarina exports; Brazil suspended chicken exports to multiple markets as a precaution.
notes: ニューカッスル病は主に家禽の疾病であり、ヒト感染は稀で軽度の結膜炎程度とされる。動物衛生当局による防疫措置と貿易制限（中国・メキシコ・チリによる輸入禁止）が中心の事案で、公衆衛生上の深刻な脅威とは言えない。ブラジル国内の家禽産業・貿易への影響として注視する価値はある。

articleSummary: Nigeria confirms its first Ebola infection in 12 years, in Abuja, a female patient with recent travel to Uganda who tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain on Oct 20. articleSummary: Thailand reports a surge in influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) during the late rainy season to early winter (week 11–17 Oct 2026). Weekly influenza cases reached 15,309; cumulative 543,385. RSV weekly cases were 2,860, cumulative 26,160. Influenza shows highest incidence in 5–9 years, then 1–4 years, and under 1 year; RSV peaks in 1–4 years, then under 1 year and 5–9 years. RSV causes severe lower respiratory illness in young children, with fever, cough, wheeze, dyspnea, and possible bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Transmission occurs via droplets and contact; diagnosis relies on history, exam, and nasal tests; imaging may be used in severe cases. Treatment is supportive; antibiotics only for bacterial co-infection. Palivizumab monoclonal antibody reduces severity, requiring monthly injections during outbreaks. Prevention emphasizes strict hygiene, handwashing, masks, cleaning toys, isolating ill individuals, avoiding crowds, and temporarily excluding sick children from nursery/school.
